compare.gravityMore: You would weigh {ratio, number} times as much as on Earth!
compare.gravityMore@simple: If you weigh 30 kg on Earth, you would weigh {kg, number} kg there!
compare.gravityMore@advanced: Surface gravity is {ratio, number} times Earth’s: your weight would grow, but your mass would stay the same.
compare.gravitySimilar: You would weigh about the same as on Earth.
compare.gravitySimilar@simple: You would feel just as heavy as on Earth.
compare.gravitySimilar@advanced: Surface gravity is within 5 % of Earth’s.
compare.gravityLess: You would weigh only {percent, number, ::percent} of your weight on Earth.
compare.gravityLess@simple: If you weigh 30 kg on Earth, you would weigh only {kg, number} kg there!
compare.gravityLess@advanced: Surface gravity is {percent, number, ::percent} of Earth’s: your weight would drop, but your mass would stay the same.

time.tooFast@simple: {body} goes around {parentId, select, sun {the Sun} other {{parent}}} {count, plural, one {# time} other {# times}} every second! That is too fast to see properly.

travel.title: Travel in time
travel.arrival: Time stops when you arrive. Press play to run on.
travel.range: Any day from the year {first} to {last}. You arrive at noon (UTC).

galileoMoons.name: Galileo sees Jupiter’s moons
galileoMoons.description: The first moons ever found around another planet.

uranusFound.name: Uranus is discovered
uranusFound.description: William Herschel finds the first planet unknown to the ancients.

neptuneFound.name: Neptune is discovered
neptuneFound.description: Found right where mathematics predicted it would be.

sputnik.name: Sputnik 1 launches
sputnik.description: The first artificial satellite starts the space age.

moonLanding.name: First Moon landing
moonLanding.description: Apollo 11 touches down on the Moon.

voyagerLaunch.name: Voyager 2 sets off
voyagerLaunch.description: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune line up for a Grand Tour, as they do only every 175 years or so.

voyagerNeptune.name: Voyager 2 reaches Neptune
voyagerNeptune.description: Twelve years after launch: the only visit Neptune has ever had.

marsClosest.name: Mars at its closest
marsClosest.description: Mars comes nearer to Earth than in almost 60,000 years. Earth sits between the Sun and Mars.

venusTransit.name: Transit of Venus
venusTransit.description: Venus passes right between the Sun and Earth.

greatConjunction.name: The great conjunction
greatConjunction.description: Seen from Earth, Jupiter and Saturn nearly touch in the sky.

nextVenusTransit.name: The next transit of Venus
nextVenusTransit.description: The next time Venus crosses in front of the Sun. Will anyone in this room see it?

spin.label: Spin

hint.realistic: Every planet turns at its true speed for the clock, so day and night match the date.
hint.realistic@simple: The planets spin exactly as fast as in real life.
hint.slowed: Spinning slowed down so that Earth turns at most once every {seconds, number} seconds. Orbits keep their speed; the other planets stay faster or slower than Earth.
hint.slowed@simple: The planets spin slower, so you can still see them turn when time runs fast. Earth takes at least {seconds, number} seconds for one turn.
hint.slow: Spinning slowed down so that Earth turns at most once every {seconds, number} seconds: slow enough to watch a single day pass. Orbits keep their speed.
hint.slow@simple: The planets spin very slowly, so you can watch one day go by. Earth takes at least {seconds, number} seconds for one turn.
hint.stopped: No planet spins, so the seasons are easy to follow as the planets travel round the Sun. Moons still keep one face toward their planet.
hint.stopped@simple: The planets stop spinning. They still travel round the Sun.

spin.notice: Not true to the clock: day and night on the planets no longer match the date.
spin.notice@simple: The planets spin slower than in real life.

info.distance: {parentId, select, sun {Distance to the Sun} other {Distance to {parent}}}
info.synchronous: always the same face toward {parentId, select, other {{parent}}}
info.synchronous@simple: always shows {parentId, select, other {{parent}}} the same side

light.openHint: Send a flash of light and watch how long it takes to cross the solar system
light.title: Watch light crawl
light.intro: Nothing is faster than light: {speed, number} km every second. Send a flash and see how long it still takes to cross the solar system.
light.intro@simple: Nothing is faster than light. It could go round the Earth 7 times in one second! Send a flash of light and see how long it takes to reach the planets.
light.intro@advanced: Light travels at exactly {speed, number} km/s. Send a pulse and watch it cross the solar system at that speed, in real time.
light.travelling@simple: The light has been on its way for
light.waiting: Time has run back to before the flash was sent.

clock.realTime: Real time: one second here is one second in real life.
clock.realTime@simple: Real time: exactly as fast as in real life.
clock.fast: Sped up to {speed}. The clock still counts the light's true travel time.
clock.fast@simple: Time is running faster than real life ({speed}). The clock still shows how long the light really needs.
clock.reversed: Time runs backwards, so the light shrinks back to where it came from.
clock.paused: Time is paused, and the light with it.

light.announce: Reached {id, select, sun {the Sun} moon {the Moon} other {{body}}} after {duration}.
light.announce@simple: The light is at {id, select, sun {the Sun} moon {the Moon} other {{body}}}! It took {duration}.
light.leftPlanets: The light has passed every planet. At this speed it reaches the nearest star in {years, number} years.
light.leftPlanets@simple: The light has passed all the planets. To reach the nearest star it needs {years, number} more years!

delay.intro: Radio signals travel at the speed of light too. This is how long a message from Earth takes right now.
delay.intro@simple: Radio messages are as fast as light, but not faster. This is how long a message from Earth needs.
delay.range: Depending on where both are in their orbits, it takes between {min} and {max}.
delay.range@simple: The planets move, so this changes: from {min} to {max}.
delay.rover: Driving a rover there from Earth? You would see where it was {oneWay} ago, and it would get your command {oneWay} later: you would be steering {roundTrip} into the past. {id, select, moon {With a few seconds that still works: Soviet teams drove the Lunokhod rovers on the Moon from Earth.} mars {That is why the rovers on Mars drive themselves.} other {That is why spacecraft that far away must steer themselves.}}
delay.rover@simple: Imagine steering a robot there with a remote control. Every button you press takes {oneWay} to get there, and you only see what happened {oneWay} later. {id, select, moon {On the Moon that is just a few seconds, so people really did drive robots there from Earth.} mars {That is why the robots on Mars have to drive by themselves.} other {That is why robots out there have to steer themselves.}}
delay.watch: Send a signal from Earth and watch

beyond.intro: The planets are only our neighbourhood. Beyond them, even light needs years.
beyond.intro@simple: The planets are only our neighbours. Everything farther away is so far that even light needs years!

proximaCentauri.name: Proxima Centauri, the nearest star
proximaCentauri.text: Its light is {duration} old when it reaches us. We see the star as it was back then.
proximaCentauri.text@simple: Its light needs {duration} to get to us.

galacticCentre.name: The centre of the Milky Way
galacticCentre.text: Its light has been travelling for {duration}. When it set off, people were still hunting mammoths.
galacticCentre.text@simple: Its light needs {duration}. When it set off, people were still hunting mammoths!

andromeda.name: The Andromeda galaxy
andromeda.text: Its light has been travelling for {duration}. When it set off, our ancestors were making the first stone tools.
andromeda.text@simple: Its light needs {duration}. When it set off, there were no people yet – only our very early ancestors.
